title: Indifference
hook: not preferring health to sickness or long life to short, only what leads to God

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Principle and Foundation: we are made to praise, reverence and serve God, and everything else is a help or a hindrance. Your line was made for this. What did you write down about why you're here? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-two.

I don't prefer health to sickness. Say that out loud and it sounds wrong. Yet a sentence like it sits near the very start of the Spiritual Exercises, right after yesterday's foundation. Ignatius of Loyola writes that a person should not want health more than sickness, riches more than poverty, honor more than dishonor, a long life more than a short one. Read fast, it sounds cold, even alarming. Read slowly, it's asking for something else. Today's word is the one he chose for that stance, and it does not mean what it means at a dinner party.
screen: `I DON'T PREFER HEALTH TO SICKNESS?` → `RIGHT AFTER THE FOUNDATION.` → `READ IT SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: In ordinary English, indifference is a shrug. Whatever. I don't care. Ignatius means nearly the opposite. Go back to yesterday: we are made, he says, to praise, reverence and serve God, and the other things on the face of the earth are made to help us toward that end. Then comes the hinge. Use things as far as they help, and let them go as far as they hinder. To do that, he says, we have to make ourselves indifferent to all created things, wherever our free choice is allowed. Notice that last part. He isn't telling anyone to skip their medicine or turn down every raise. Where the choice isn't free, there is nothing to weigh. Where it is free, indifference keeps the scale level until you can see which way leads toward God. Then you choose, with your whole self. So this is not a lack of feeling. It's balance before a decision. A person can want health very badly and still hold that wanting open. Saint Paul says something close in his letter to the Philippians, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, to be content therewith." Learned. It took practice. And Ignatius ends his sentence with the point of the whole thing: desiring and choosing only what leads more to the end for which we are made. Some readers find the word itself a trap, because it sounds like numbness, and some teachers reach for other words instead: freedom, availability, open hands. In a real week it can look like this. A job offer in another city. A worrying test result. A grown child choosing a path you didn't pick. Indifference doesn't make the feelings vanish. It lets them speak, then asks one more question: which of these helps me love God and the people in front of me?
screen: `NOT A SHRUG.` · `USE THINGS AS FAR AS THEY HELP.` · `WHERE OUR FREE CHOICE IS ALLOWED.` · `BALANCE BEFORE A DECISION.` · then, large: `CONTENT IN WHATSOEVER STATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one preference loosely. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you want right now. A real one, not a huge one: a reply to a message, a quiet weekend, the result of a test. Rest your hands open on your knees. Name the preference silently: I'd like this. Then add: and if it goes the other way, I can still walk toward what matters. Don't force the feeling to change. Just notice whether your grip loosens a little as you breathe. If you pray, you can offer the preference to God and leave it there for the length of this sit. The bell holds the time.
Indifference. In Ignatius's sense, not a shrug but a balance: holding created things open until you can see which way leads to God. Today's word.
Your line: hold it loosely. Today, when something you wanted doesn't happen, a parking spot, a plan, a yes, say the line once before you react. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: In Ignatian retreats, people pray for this inner freedom, which Ignatius calls indifference, before making a major decision, often with the help of a spiritual director.

fork.setup: you're offered a better job in another city, and you want it badly. on Ignatius's terms, what comes first?
options: take it: wanting it is the sign.
refuse it: wanting it is the danger.
hold it open, and ask which way leads toward God.
fork.reveal: the Exercises ask for balance first, then a whole-hearted choice. the wanting isn't wrong; it just isn't the only thing weighed.

original.note: Spanish, the language Ignatius wrote the Exercises in: indifferent, balanced, not yet leaning either way.

trapdoor: what you thought: indifference means not caring.
what it means: in the Exercises, it's holding health, money, honor and long life open, so you can choose what leads to God.
what a scholar hears: it follows straight from the Principle and Foundation, and Ignatius limits it to matters left to our free choice.

sources.quoted: I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, to be content therewith.

notes: The Principle and Foundation is paraphrased (health/sickness, riches/poverty, honor/dishonor, long/short life; 'in so far as it is allowed to our free choice'); no translation of the Exercises is quoted. Confirm the paraphrase.
Douay-Rheims wording of Philippians 4:11 to confirm.
Original: Spanish 'indiferentes' as in the autograph ('hacernos indiferentes'); confirm spelling and pronunciation.
'Some teachers reach for other words: freedom, availability, open hands' is a soft, unattributed claim; confirm it is fair.
